summary: Designed the operator TUI and committed 90 RED tests pinning it. Module split under apps/cli/src/tui: one impure function (runTuiShell) and eight pure modules. Render contract is renderFrame(state, viewport) -> plain text lines of exactly the viewport's shape, no ANSI, deterministic. Input model is mapKey -> Intent -> reduce -> effect descriptions, with the trust gate in the reducer. 87 of 90 tests fail on named NOT_IMPLEMENTED stubs; the other 3 lock exported contract constants. Every test was proven satisfiable by a throwaway probe (90/90 green), which was then reverted and the tree verified by SHA-256. pnpm typecheck stays green on 7 projects. Concern: the dispatch premise that the reference TUI has no UI dependency is incorrect - it depends on @opentui/core as an optional, type-only dependency; the transferable property is dependency inversion, not absence, and that is what was adopted.

findings.problem: The dispatch states the reference TUI at /home/altsay/keryx/src/tui has 'no UI dependency whatsoever - only Node builtins'. The source says otherwise: shell-chrome.ts declares '@opentui/core is an OPTIONAL dependency (ADR-0005)' and types its renderables as typeof import("@opentui/core"), with a static regex guard forbidding the literal import form in runtime modules. modal-host.test.ts loads the real package through a try/catch and skips when it is absent.
findings.impact: The premise attributes the reference's testability to the wrong cause. If an implementer copies 'no dependency' without copying 'no static coupling to a renderer, everything injected at the I/O edge', they can still write an untestable TUI - the reference is testable because state-to-lines is pure and the renderer arrives as a parameter, not because a package.json is short. Acting on the stated premise alone risks losing the property AC5 and AC6 depend on.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the corrected reason in the flow journal alongside the original note. The design note section 2 states it, and the design adopts the transferable property (dependency inversion plus pure formatters) while still adding no UI package, as the dispatch requires.
findings.evidence: SSH read-only inspection of geekom:/home/altsay/keryx/src/tui/shell-chrome.ts lines 38-56 and modal-host.test.ts lines 1-40. Nothing on geekom was modified.

findings.problem: AC5 requires the surface to show pinned contacts, but the frozen eight-command CLI surface has no command that lists them. doctor returns contact_count only; Profile.listContacts() exists in the runtime with no entry point, like rotateBundle() and retryPending().
findings.impact: The two obvious resolutions are both wrong. Adding 'contact list' is the ninth command specification.md deliberately froze the surface against. Reading the encrypted store directly from the TUI would require the TUI to hold the 32-byte store key - precisely what AC5 forbids - so the convenient fix is the one that breaks the criterion being satisfied.
findings.suggested_fix: Adopted: the TUI lists the contacts this session observed (exported or imported through the trust modal, whose four identifiers it already had to display), cross-checks the count against doctor's contact_count, and states the shortfall explicitly rather than showing a plausible list that is silently short. Pinned by profiles-pane.test.ts.

class_scope.enumeration_method: The class is 'runtime capability with no CLI entry point', and it is enumerated by construction rather than by search: commandOptions in cli.ts:87-96 is the single dispatch table, parseCommand refuses any positional string absent from it, and specification.md names the frozen surface as exactly those eight. So every public runtime method not reachable from one of the eight switch arms in execute() is a member. specification.md already names rotateBundle and retryPending as deliberate members; listContacts and retryPendingAcks are the two further members, found by reading the public methods of Profile, OutboundMessenger and InboundMessenger against those switch arms (keryx ctx rg over apps/cli/src). The set is exhaustive for those three classes.

findings.problem: send passes the message body as --text <plaintext>, so message plaintext appears in the child's argument vector and is visible in the local process table for the life of that process.
findings.impact: None of the AC5 assertions in this task cover it, and none claim to: they are about key material. Reported so the evidence is not read as proving more than it does. The exposure is the existing CLI contract, which the runbook drives the same way; the TUI inherits it rather than creating it.
findings.suggested_fix: Out of scope for T9 - closing it needs a change to send's interface or a ninth entry point, both of which reopen the frozen-surface decision. Recorded in the design note section 6 so a later flow can weigh it deliberately.

findings.problem: Eight declaration stubs were committed alongside the tests, rather than leaving the modules absent. apps/cli/tsconfig.json includes src/**/*, so tests importing non-existent modules would turn pnpm typecheck red for the whole project.
findings.impact: Without the stubs the RED phase reports as a compile failure rather than as failing expectations, and the stated baseline (typecheck green on 7 projects) would break for reasons unrelated to the implementation. With them, every test fails on a named NOT_IMPLEMENTED and typecheck stays green.
findings.suggested_fix: The implementer replaces each stub body and deletes apps/cli/src/tui/not-implemented.ts, whose header says exactly that. No behaviour was written: every stub function body is a single call to notImplemented(name, ...args).
findings.evidence: apps/cli/src/tui/not-implemented.ts; pnpm -r typecheck green on 7 projects after the tests were added.

findings.problem: Three of the 90 tests pass in the RED phase because they assert over exported contract constants the stubs already carry: the eight-command list, the four trust identifier names and order, and the wording of UNAUDITED_NOTICE.
findings.impact: They are contract locks rather than RED tests, and must not be counted as evidence that the implementation exists. A fourth would have joined them - a bare expect(...).toThrow() on an unsupported command was satisfied by the NOT_IMPLEMENTED scaffold itself - and was tightened to require the refusal to name the command it refused.
findings.suggested_fix: None needed; the distinction is recorded so the RED evidence is read correctly. 87 of 90 fail on named missing implementations.
findings.evidence: vitest run src/tui after restore: 87 failed of 90. The passing three are cli-bridge 'declares exactly the eight commands', modal-host 'names exactly the four fields', shell-chrome 'states both halves of the warning'.
